why_how.text: Graduated Driver Licensing pairs two driver education segments with three license levels, adding privileges step by step until age eighteen.
Segment two builds on Segment one and on real driving time, so it needs a supervised log and three months on Level one first.

scenario.text: Leo finished Segment one, has held Level one for three months, and has logged thirty supervised hours, two at night.

reasoning.text: Segment two entry needs at least thirty supervised hours with two at night and three consecutive months on Level one.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the Segment two exam has a higher passing score than Segment one.

correction.text: Both state exams share the same minimum score of seventy percent.

prompt.text: A student wants to know the minimum score for the Segment two state exam. What is it?

rationale.text: Segment two's state exam needs at least seventy percent, the same minimum as Segment one.

lines.text: Two driver education segments.
Three license levels.
It ends at eighteen.

narration.text: Welcome to Graduated Driver Licensing, the path Michigan teens follow to a full license. The program combines two driver education segments with requirements for three license levels, adds privileges at each level, and ends when you turn eighteen. This first lesson focuses on the two segments, the classroom and driving training that sit underneath the license levels. Segment numbers, hours and scores are favorite targets for practice questions, because they are easy to swap. We will go through each one carefully so you can keep them straight when the options look alike.

lines.text: Start at fourteen years, eight months.
Parent or guardian permission needed.

narration.text: You may start driver education Segment one at fourteen years, eight months old, with a parent's or guardian's permission. That date matters because it comes just before the earliest age for the Level one Learner's License, which is one month later. So the order is natural: you begin the classroom work first, and the license follows. Keep the permission requirement in mind too. A question may describe a student who is old enough but has no parent or guardian approval, and that student is not ready to start the segment.

lines.text: Twenty-four classroom hours or more.
Six hours behind the wheel.
Four hours observing.

narration.text: Segment one has three time requirements. It takes at least twenty-four hours in the classroom, at least six hours behind the wheel, and at least four hours observing from a training vehicle. Finishing it also requires a score of at least seventy percent on the Segment one state exam. A helpful way to remember the hours is the countdown twenty-four, six, four: the classroom total is largest, driving comes next, and observing is smallest. If a question shows six classroom hours, that number belongs to Segment two, not Segment one.

lines.text: Thirty supervised hours, two at night.
Three consecutive months on Level one.
Six classroom hours, seventy percent exam.

narration.text: Segment two comes after you have some real driving behind you. To enter it, you need a log showing at least thirty supervised hours, at least two of them at night, and at least three consecutive months holding the Level one license. Segment two itself includes at least six hours of classroom instruction, and its state exam must be passed with at least seventy percent. Notice how much shorter the classroom part is than Segment one. The focus has shifted to the driving you have logged, which is why the log is an entry requirement.

lines.text: Trap: Segment two needs a higher score.
Both exams need seventy percent.
Twenty-four classroom hours is Segment one.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because Segment two comes later, people assume it must be harder to pass. It is not. The Segment one and Segment two driver education state exams share the same minimum score of seventy percent. A second trap swaps the classroom hours. Segment one needs at least twenty-four classroom hours, while Segment two needs at least six. And watch the hours in the log: thirty supervised hours with two at night is the Segment two entry rule, which is less than the fifty hours needed later for the skills test. Match each number to its step.

lines.text: Segment two state exam.
What is the minimum score?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a student is getting ready for the Segment two state exam and wants to know the minimum passing score. What is it? Recall the rule that links the two segments. Both driver education state exams use the same minimum, seventy percent. So the answer is seventy percent for Segment two, exactly as for Segment one. If you guessed something higher because Segment two comes later, that is the trap from the last slide. The sequence of the segments changes the hours and the entry requirements, but not the minimum exam score.

lines.text: Start at fourteen and eight months.
Twenty-four, six, four for Segment one.
Thirty hours and three months for Segment two.

narration.text: To wrap up the segments, here is the whole picture. Graduated Driver Licensing combines two segments and three levels and ends at eighteen. Segment one may start at fourteen years, eight months with permission, and it takes at least twenty-four classroom hours, six behind the wheel and four observing, finished with a seventy percent exam. Segment two needs a log of thirty supervised hours with two at night and three months on Level one to enter, then at least six classroom hours and another seventy percent exam. Both segment exams need seventy.

why_how.text: Level one lets a teen drive only with a licensed adult beside them, which is how the supervised hours in the log are built.
A supervising adult other than the parent needs the parent's signed letter, so the parent stays in control of who supervises.

scenario.text: Nina's neighbor, a licensed twenty-four-year-old, offers to supervise her Level one practice drive.

reasoning.text: A designated licensed adult aged twenty-one or older may supervise, but only with a signed authorization letter from the parent or guardian.

result.text: The neighbor may supervise once he carries the signed letter from Nina's parent.

claim.text: Myth: the Learner's License can be issued as soon as Segment one starts, at fourteen years and eight months.

correction.text: Segment one can start at fourteen years, eight months, but Level one cannot be issued until fourteen years, nine months.

prompt.text: A licensed adult who is not the parent wants to supervise a Level one driver. What three things must be true?

answer.text: They must be licensed, at least twenty-one, and carry the parent's signed authorization letter.

rationale.text: A designated adult needs a license, an age of twenty-one or older, and the parent's or guardian's signed letter.

lines.text: Level one is the Learner's License.
Always supervised, never on the phone.

narration.text: This lesson covers the Level one Learner's License, the first license step for Michigan teens. It is the level where you learn by driving with an experienced adult beside you every time. We will go through who can get it, what you bring to the office, who may supervise you and what they need, how the supervised driving log works, and the rule about phones. Many practice questions here turn on small details such as the exact age, the age of the supervising adult and whether a letter is needed, so we will slow down on each of them.

lines.text: Minimum age fourteen years, nine months.
Office visit with a parent or guardian.
Pass vision and health standards.

narration.text: The Level one Learner's License needs a minimum age of fourteen years, nine months, an office visit together with a parent or legal guardian, and passing the vision and health standards. At the office you bring the Segment one Certificate of Completion plus proof of a valid Social Security number or an ineligibility letter, U.S. citizenship or legal presence, identity and Michigan residency. Notice that Segment one has to be finished first, since its certificate is on the list. This is why the start of Segment one comes a little earlier than the Level one age.

lines.text: Licensed parent or guardian.
Or a designated licensed adult twenty-one or older.
Designated adults carry a signed letter.

narration.text: With a Level one license you may drive only when a licensed parent, guardian, or designated licensed adult aged twenty-one or older sits in the front seat beside you. If the supervising adult is not your parent or guardian, they need a signed authorization letter from your parent or guardian. So three conditions stack for a designated adult: licensed, at least twenty-one, and carrying the letter. A licensed nineteen-year-old does not qualify, and neither does an unlicensed adult. The front seat placement matters as well, because the adult must be beside you.

lines.text: Log at least fifty hours, ten at night.
Kelsey's Law: no phone for Level one.

narration.text: While on Level one you keep a supervised driving log. Before the driving skills test you must reach at least fifty hours, ten of them at night. The log is your proof, so it travels with you to the test. There is also a strict phone rule. Kelsey's Law bars a Level one driver from using a cell phone while driving. That ban is simpler than the Level two phone rule you will learn later, so do not borrow the Level two exception here. For a Level one driver, using a cell phone while driving is not allowed. Keep the two rules separate in your mind.

lines.text: Photo hard card at Level one.
Skip the office visit for Level two.
Regular license mailed at eighteen.

narration.text: Some teens receive a photo hard card for Level one. A teen given a hard card skips the office visit for Level two, and the regular operator's license is mailed when that teen turns eighteen. That saves a trip later, because the card already carries what the office needs. Teens with a paper card take a different route that you will see in the Level two lesson. For now, the key idea is that the type of card you receive at Level one affects whether you need to return to an office when you move up to the next level. Ask which card the teen holds.

lines.text: Trap: Learner's License at Segment one start.
Segment one: fourteen years, eight months.
Level one: fourteen years, nine months.

narration.text: Here is a trap that catches careful readers. The Segment one start age and the Level one license age are close, but not the same. Segment one can begin at fourteen years, eight months, but the Level one Learner's License cannot be issued until fourteen years, nine months, so the two ages differ by one month. A second trap is about supervisors. A supervising adult who is not the parent or guardian must be licensed, at least twenty-one, and carry the parent's signed authorization letter. Missing any one of those three conditions means that adult cannot supervise you.

lines.text: Not the parent.
What must they have?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a licensed adult who is not the teen's parent or guardian wants to supervise a Level one drive. What three things must be true about that adult? Bring together the supervision rules. The adult must hold a license, must be at least twenty-one years old, and must carry a signed authorization letter from the parent or guardian. If any of the three is missing, the teen may not drive with that adult. A licensed eighteen-year-old cousin with a letter still fails the age rule, and a licensed adult without the letter fails too.

lines.text: Fourteen years, nine months, with a parent.
Licensed adult twenty-one or older beside you.
Fifty hours, ten at night; no phone.

narration.text: To close Level one, remember the essentials. The Learner's License needs age fourteen years, nine months, an office visit with a parent or guardian, vision and health standards, and the Segment one certificate plus four kinds of proof. You may drive only with a licensed parent, guardian or designated licensed adult aged twenty-one or older in the front seat, and a designated adult carries the parent's signed letter. Keep a log of at least fifty hours, ten at night, before the skills test. Kelsey's Law bars cell phone use. Hard-card teens skip the Level two visit.

why_how.text: The skills test checks a teen's readiness after training, so it waits for age fifteen, Segment two, fifty logged hours and six months on Level one.

scenario.text: Sam is fifteen, finished Segment two, held Level one for six months, and logged fifty hours with ten at night.

reasoning.text: The skills test needs all four conditions: age fifteen, Segment two finished, fifty hours with ten at night, and six months on Level one.

result.text: Sam may take the driving skills test.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the thirty logged hours that opened Segment two are enough for the skills test.

correction.text: The Segment two log needs thirty hours with two at night, while the skills test needs the full fifty hours with ten at night.

prompt.text: A fifteen-year-old has finished Segment two and held Level one for six months, but logged only thirty hours. May they take the skills test?

answer.text: No. The skills test needs at least fifty hours, ten at night.

rationale.text: Thirty hours only opens Segment two; the skills test needs fifty supervised hours with ten at night.

lines.text: Four conditions must all be met.
Bring the right papers.

narration.text: This short lesson is about the driving skills test, the road test that stands between Level one and Level two for Michigan teens. There are four conditions you must meet before you can take it, and a set of documents you must show on test day. The conditions repeat numbers you have seen before, which is exactly why they get mixed up. Hours in the log, months on Level one, and age all appear here again, but with different values than the earlier steps. We will line them up so you can spot the correct combination right away.

lines.text: At least fifteen years old.
Segment two finished.
Fifty hours, ten at night; six months on Level one.

narration.text: To take the driving skills test you must be at least fifteen, have finished Segment two, have the fifty supervised hours with ten at night, and have held Level one for at least six months. All four must be true at the same time. A fifteen-year-old who has not finished Segment two must wait. A student who finished Segment two but has only held Level one for three months must wait too. Think of it as a checklist that you complete line by line. If even one line is missing, the test has to wait until it is filled in. No shortcut skips a line.

lines.text: Completed driving log and Level one license.
Segment two certificate.
Insurance and registration for the test vehicle.

narration.text: On test day you show several things. You bring the completed log, your Level one license, the Segment two certificate, and insurance and registration for the test vehicle. Approved driver testing businesses give the test, so you schedule with one of them rather than with a classroom instructor. The log is especially important, because it is the proof of your fifty hours. Without it, the test cannot show you met that condition. The vehicle papers matter too, since you are driving that vehicle during the test and it must be insured and registered.

lines.text: Trap: thirty hours is enough.
Thirty with two at night opens Segment two.
Fifty with ten at night unlocks the test.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two different hour counts appear on the way to Level two. The Segment two log needs thirty supervised hours with two at night, while the skills test needs the full fifty hours with ten at night. A tricky question may describe a student with thirty hours and ask whether they can test. They cannot, because thirty hours only opens Segment two. A similar swap uses time on Level one: three consecutive months gets you into Segment two, but the skills test needs six months. Read both the hours and the months in every option.

lines.text: Fifteen, Segment two done, six months.
Only thirty hours logged.
Ready to test?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a fifteen-year-old has finished Segment two and has held Level one for six months, but the log shows only thirty supervised hours. May they take the driving skills test? Work through the checklist. Age fifteen is met, Segment two is met, and six months on Level one is met. The hours are not. The skills test needs at least fifty supervised hours with ten at night, and thirty hours only opened Segment two. So the answer is no, not yet. Once the log reaches fifty hours with ten at night, the test is open.

lines.text: Fifteen, Segment two, fifty hours, six months.
Bring log, license, certificate, vehicle papers.
Thirty then fifty.

narration.text: To close, here are the skills test rules in one place. You must be at least fifteen, have finished Segment two, have logged fifty supervised hours with ten at night, and have held Level one for at least six months. On test day you show the completed log, your Level one license, the Segment two certificate, and the test vehicle's insurance and registration, and an approved driver testing business gives the test. Keep the hour counts in order: thirty supervised hours with two at night opens Segment two, then fifty with ten at night opens the skills test.

why_how.text: Level two adds driving alone but keeps night, passenger and phone limits, each with specific exceptions.
The type of Level one card decides the path: hard-card teens advance automatically, paper-card teens bring documents to an office.

scenario.text: Jada, on Level two, drives her two younger brothers home from school at four in the afternoon.

reasoning.text: Immediate family passengers are an exception to the passenger limit, and the night limit only runs from ten p.m. to five a.m.

claim.text: Many people think immediate family passengers also excuse a Level two driver from the night limit.

correction.text: Immediate family is an exception to the passenger limit, but it is not listed as an exception to the night driving limit.

prompt.text: A Level two driver wants to drive a sibling to a movie that ends at eleven at night, with no adult along. Is the drive home allowed?

answer.text: No. Family passengers are not an exception to the ten p.m. to five a.m. limit.

rationale.text: The night limit has its own exceptions, and immediate family passengers are not one of them.

lines.text: Level two adds independence.
Night, passenger and phone limits remain.

narration.text: Level two, the Intermediate License, is where a Michigan teen first drives without a supervising adult. That freedom comes with three limits: one about night driving, one about passengers, and one about phones. Each limit has its own exceptions, and practice questions love to borrow an exception from one limit and apply it to another. In this lesson we will cover how you qualify for Level two, the two different ways teens move up depending on their card, and then each limit with its exceptions. Pay attention to which exception belongs to which rule.

lines.text: Age sixteen.
Six months on Level one.
Clean ninety days before applying.

narration.text: The Level two Intermediate License requires age sixteen, at least six months on Level one, and a record clear of violations, at-fault crashes and suspensions for the ninety days before you apply. That ninety-day look-back is shorter than the one you will see for Level three. You also must have passed the driving skills test. Notice how the earlier requirements feed this one: the six months on Level one is the same span the skills test needed. If a question describes a teen with a recent at-fault crash, check whether it falls inside those ninety days.

lines.text: Hard card: move up automatically.
Paper card: office visit with documents.

narration.text: How you move up depends on your Level one card. Hard-card teens who meet the Level two requirements and have passed the skills test move up to Level two automatically. Paper-card teens must visit an office with their Level one license, Segment two certificate, Driving Skills Test Certificate and the Social Security, legal presence, identity and residency documents described in the state's form. So the paper card means one more trip. The requirements themselves are the same for both groups. Only the process of getting the Level two license is different.

lines.text: No driving ten p.m. to five a.m. without an exception.
One passenger under twenty-one at any hour.

narration.text: A Level two driver may not drive from ten p.m. to five a.m. unless a parent, guardian or designated licensed adult aged twenty-one or older is along, or the trip is for work, to or from work, or to or from an authorized activity. A Level two driver may also carry at most one passenger under twenty-one, unless a parent, guardian or designated adult aged twenty-one or older rides along, the passengers are immediate family, or the trip is for work or an authorized activity. Notice that the passenger list includes immediate family, and the night list does not.

lines.text: Kelsey's Law: phone only in an emergency.
Violations can bring fines or community service.

narration.text: Kelsey's Law also covers Level two. It forbids a Level two driver from using a phone except in an emergency, and a violation could bring a civil infraction with fines, community service or both. Compare this with Level one, where the rule simply bars cell phone use while driving. At Level two the stated exception is an emergency, and nothing else. So a red light, a quick text or a passenger holding the phone does not create a new exception. When a question asks what a Level two driver may do with a phone, the safe answer is emergency use only.

lines.text: Trap: family excuses the night limit.
Family is a passenger exception only.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Immediate family passengers are an exception to the Level two passenger limit, but they are not listed as an exception to the night driving limit. So a Level two driver may take two younger siblings to school in the afternoon, because family passengers are allowed. But driving those same siblings home at eleven at night, with no qualifying adult and no work or authorized activity, is still a night violation. Another trap concerns how teens move up. Hard-card teens advance automatically, while paper-card teens must bring their documents to a Secretary of State office.

lines.text: Level two driver with a sibling.
Movie ends at eleven at night.
No adult along.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a Level two driver takes a younger sibling to a movie, and the drive home starts at eleven at night with no parent, guardian or designated adult in the car. The trip is not for work or an authorized activity. Is the drive home allowed? Separate the two limits. The passenger part is fine, since immediate family is a passenger exception. The night part is not. Driving from ten p.m. to five a.m. needs a qualifying adult, work or an authorized activity, and family passengers are not on that list. So the answer is no.

lines.text: Sixteen, six months, clean ninety days.
No ten to five without an exception.
One young passenger; phone for emergencies.

narration.text: To finish Level two, here is the summary. You need age sixteen, at least six months on Level one, a passed skills test and a clean record for the ninety days before applying. Hard-card teens move up automatically, while paper-card teens visit an office with their documents. Without an exception, a Level two driver may not drive from ten p.m. to five a.m. and may carry at most one passenger under twenty-one. Immediate family excuses the passenger limit but not the night limit. Under Kelsey's Law, phone use is allowed only in an emergency.

why_how.text: Level three removes state restrictions, so it requires a longer clean record than Level two: twelve consecutive months instead of ninety days.

scenario.text: Theo is seventeen, has held Level two for eight months, and has had no violations, crashes or suspensions in the last twelve months.

reasoning.text: Level three needs age seventeen, six months on Level two, and twelve consecutive clean months, with parental authorization.

result.text: Theo's Level three license is issued automatically and free, unless a parent asks to delay it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking Level three uses the same ninety-day clean-record window as Level two.

correction.text: Applying for GDL Level two requires ninety days free of violations, at-fault crashes, and suspensions, whereas GDL Level three requires holding Level two at least six months and driving twelve consecutive months without a moving violation, at-fault crash, suspension, or GDL restriction violation.

prompt.text: A seventeen-year-old has held Level two for seven months but had an at-fault crash ten months ago. Do they qualify for Level three yet?

answer.text: No. Level three needs twelve consecutive months with no at-fault crash.

rationale.text: Level three's clean-record rule covers twelve consecutive months, so a crash ten months ago still blocks it.

lines.text: Level three is the Full License.
No state restrictions.

narration.text: This lesson covers Level three, the Full License, the final step of Graduated Driver Licensing. Once you reach it, the state restrictions you followed on Level one and Level two no longer apply. Getting there depends on age, time on Level two, and a clean driving record over a long stretch. The tricky part is that Level two and Level three both have clean-record rules, but they look back over very different lengths of time. We will also put the ages for the skills test, Level two and Level three side by side so the ladder is easy to remember.

lines.text: Age seventeen.
Six months on Level two.
Twelve clean consecutive months.

narration.text: The Level three Full License requires age seventeen, at least six months on Level two, and twelve consecutive months with no moving violation, at-fault crash, suspension or GDL restriction violation. That last part includes breaking the Level two limits you learned, like the night or passenger rules. So a teen who carried too many passengers during that year has not yet met the requirement. All three conditions must be true together. Turning seventeen alone is not enough, and neither is a clean year if the teen has only held Level two for a few months.

lines.text: Issued automatically and free.
Needs parental authorization.
A parent may ask to delay it.

narration.text: Level three is issued automatically and free once the requirements are met with parental authorization. It carries no state restrictions, and it may be delayed at a parent's or guardian's request. That last point surprises some learners. Even when a teen meets every requirement, a parent or guardian can ask for the Full License to wait. There is no extra test and no fee for the upgrade itself. So if a question describes a teen paying for a Level three road test, that is not how this step works. The upgrade comes on its own.

lines.text: Trap: Level three uses ninety days.
Level two: clean ninety days.
Level three: twelve clean months.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Applying for GDL Level two requires ninety days free of violations, at-fault crashes, and suspensions, whereas GDL Level three requires holding Level two at least six months and driving twelve consecutive months without a moving violation, at-fault crash, suspension, or GDL restriction violation. It is easy to carry the ninety-day number forward. Another trap is the age ladder. The minimum ages climb by level: fifteen for the skills test, sixteen for Level two, and seventeen for Level three. Questions may shift every age down by one or up by one, so anchor yourself with fifteen, sixteen, seventeen in that order. When you see a record window, ask which level it belongs to before you decide.

lines.text: Seventeen, seven months on Level two.
At-fault crash ten months ago.
Ready for Level three?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a seventeen-year-old has held Level two for seven months, but had an at-fault crash ten months ago. Do they qualify for Level three yet? Check each requirement. Age seventeen is met, and six months on Level two is met. The clean-record rule is not. Level three needs twelve consecutive months with no moving violation, at-fault crash, suspension or GDL violation, and a crash ten months ago falls inside that window. So the answer is no. Once twelve clean months have passed, Level three can be issued automatically and free.

lines.text: Seventeen, six months, twelve clean months.
Automatic, free, parent may delay.
Fifteen, sixteen, seventeen.

narration.text: To wrap up, Level three is the Full License with no state restrictions. It needs age seventeen, at least six months on Level two, and twelve consecutive months free of moving violations, at-fault crashes, suspensions and GDL restriction violations. It is issued automatically and free with parental authorization, and a parent or guardian may ask to delay it. Remember the two record windows: ninety days for Level two, twelve months for Level three. And remember the age ladder: fifteen for the skills test, sixteen for Level two, seventeen for Level three.

why_how.text: Adults who have never been licensed skip the teen program and use a temporary instruction permit before a skills test.
Adult practice is counted in days on the TIP, while the teen log counts supervised hours.
The written knowledge test is free at an office; only the online version at home carries a convenience fee.

scenario.text: Ana is twenty-two, has never held a license, and has just received her TIP.

reasoning.text: She must practice with a licensed adult for at least thirty days before the skills test given by a driver testing business.

result.text: Ana schedules her skills test at least thirty days after getting her TIP, and the license arrives by mail about three weeks after she passes.

claim.text: Myth: adult applicants must log fifty supervised hours, just like teens.

correction.text: Adults must practice at least thirty days on a TIP, a count of days, whereas the teen log counts supervised hours.

prompt.text: An adult took the written knowledge test at a Secretary of State office. What did the test itself cost?

answer.text: Nothing. The test is free at every office.

rationale.text: Only the optional online version at home carries a convenience fee; the office test costs nothing.

lines.text: Eighteen or older, never licensed.
TIP first, then a skills test.

narration.text: This lesson is for adults who have never held a license. If you are eighteen or older and have never been licensed, you do not go through the teen segments and levels. Instead you follow a shorter path built around a temporary instruction permit, called a TIP, and a driving skills test. We will cover what you bring, what the knowledge test costs, the steps that lead to your TIP, how long you must practice, and when your license arrives. Several of these steps carry numbers that differ from the teen path, so we will point those out.

lines.text: Apply for a TIP at an office.
Pass a skills test from a testing business.
Bring four proofs; pre-apply online.

narration.text: Anyone eighteen or older who has never been licensed must apply for a temporary instruction permit at a Secretary of State office and pass a skills test given by a driver testing business. Adult first-time applicants bring four proofs, covering identity, Michigan residency, U.S. citizenship or legal presence, and a valid Social Security number. Pre-applying online at Michigan dot gov slash SOS speeds up the visit. So the adult path has the same document idea as the teen path, four kinds of proof, but no driver education segments and no Level one or Level two.

lines.text: Office knowledge test is free.
Online at home costs a convenience fee.
Tests, TIP fee, photo, then TIP.

narration.text: The written knowledge test is free at every Secretary of State office, or you can take an online version at home for a six dollar and fifty cent convenience fee. Your TIP is then issued after three steps: passing the written knowledge and vision tests, paying the TIP fee, and having your photo taken. Notice that the fee you pay at the office is the TIP fee, not a charge for taking the test there. If you choose the online test at home, that is the only place the convenience fee appears. Once those three steps are done, you hold your TIP.

lines.text: Practice thirty days with a licensed adult.
Then the skills test.
License by mail in about three weeks.

narration.text: With your TIP in hand, you must practice with a licensed adult for at least thirty days before the skills test. After you pass, the license should arrive by mail in about three weeks. Thirty days is a count of calendar time, not a log of hours. That is an important difference from the teen program, which counts supervised hours instead. So an adult does not need to prove fifty logged hours. They need to have held the TIP and practiced for at least thirty days. Then the skills test from a driver testing business is the final step.

lines.text: Trap: adults log fifty hours.
Adults: thirty days on a TIP.
Teens: supervised hours in a log.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because teens log fifty supervised hours, some learners think adults must do the same. They do not. Adults must practice at least thirty days on a TIP before the skills test, a count of days, whereas the teen log counts supervised hours. A second trap is the test fee. The written knowledge test costs nothing at an office, and only the optional online version at home carries the six dollar and fifty cent convenience fee. If an option says the office test costs money, it is wrong. Look for days versus hours and office versus online.

lines.text: Knowledge test at an office.
What did the test cost?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an adult first-time applicant took the written knowledge test at a Secretary of State office. What did the test itself cost? Recall the cost rule. The written knowledge test is free at every office, and the only version with a convenience fee is the optional online test at home. So the test cost nothing. The applicant still pays the TIP fee as one of the steps before the permit is issued, but that is a different charge. If you answered the convenience fee, that belongs only to the online version taken at home.

lines.text: TIP, four proofs, free office test.
Thirty days of practice.
Skills test, then license by mail.

narration.text: To close, here is the adult path. If you are eighteen or older and never licensed, apply for a TIP at an office and later pass a skills test from a driver testing business. Bring four proofs: identity, residency, citizenship or legal presence, and a Social Security number, and pre-apply online to speed things up. The knowledge test is free at an office, with a convenience fee only for the online version. Pass the tests, pay the TIP fee and take your photo to get the TIP. Practice thirty days, pass the skills test, and expect your license by mail in about three weeks.

lines.text: Social Security, legal presence, identity, residency.
Originals, matching names, recent dates.

narration.text: This lesson is about the documents you bring when you apply. Whether you are a teen getting Level one or an adult getting a TIP, you prove the same kinds of things: your Social Security status, your legal presence, your identity and your Michigan residency. Each kind of proof has its own rules about what counts, how old it may be and whether a copy is acceptable. Many people are turned away at the counter over small document problems, and practice questions focus on exactly those details. We will go through each one in turn.

lines.text: Collected to verify status and help child support.
No number: ineligibility letter.
Letter no more than sixty days old.

narration.text: The Secretary of State collects Social Security numbers under state and federal law to verify citizenship or legal presence and to help with child support collection. If you have no Social Security number, you must present an ineligibility letter from the Social Security Administration that is no more than sixty days old. That sixty-day limit is strict. An older letter will not work, even if nothing has changed. So a person without a number is not excused from this proof. They bring a recent letter instead of the number itself.

lines.text: Certified birth certificate, passport, or listed cards.
Names and birth dates should match.
Name changes need legal proof.

narration.text: Accepted proof of legal presence includes a certified birth certificate with a raised seal from a U.S. government unit or territory, a valid unexpired U.S. passport, a citizenship or naturalization certificate, a Permanent Resident Card, or an Employment Authorization Card. Your first and last names and birth date should match across documents, and every name change needs legal proof such as an original marriage license, divorce decree or court order. So if your birth certificate shows a different last name than your current one, you bring the legal document that connects the two names.

lines.text: Original documents only.
Photocopies and faxes are refused.
Own license works if expired under four years.

narration.text: Identity proof must be original documents. Photocopies and faxes are refused, and you may need more than one document. There is one helpful allowance for people moving in. Out-of-state and Canadian applicants may use their own license as identity proof as long as it has been expired for less than four years. So a license from Ohio that expired two years ago can still prove identity, while one that expired six years ago cannot. Notice that the allowance is about identity proof only. It does not replace the other kinds of proof you bring.

lines.text: At least two documents.
Bills or statements from the last ninety days.
Family-name documents need proof of relationship.

narration.text: Residency proof takes at least two documents, such as a utility bill, credit card bill or account statement from the last ninety days, a pay stub, an earnings statement, a mortgage or lease, or an insurance policy. Residency documents in a family member's name are accepted when the family relationship is shown by other documented proof. So a young adult living with parents can use a parent's utility bill, as long as other documents show the relationship. One bill on its own is never enough, because the minimum is two documents for residency.

lines.text: Trap: the letter can be ninety days old.
Ineligibility letter: sixty days at most.
Residency bills: last ninety days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two different date limits appear in the document rules, and they are easy to swap. The Social Security ineligibility letter may be at most sixty days old, while residency bills and statements must be from the last ninety days. So a letter that is seventy-five days old is too old, even though a seventy-five-day-old utility bill would be fine for residency. Another trap is copies. Identity proof must be original, and photocopies and faxes are refused. When a question names a document, check its type, its age and whether it is an original.

lines.text: Photocopy of a passport.
Offered as identity proof.
Accepted?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an applicant hands over a clear photocopy of their valid passport as identity proof. Will it be accepted? Recall the identity rule. Identity proof must be original documents, and photocopies and faxes are refused. So the answer is no, even though the passport itself would be acceptable if the original were presented. The applicant should bring the original passport or another original document, and they may need more than one. If you answered yes because the passport is valid, remember that the form of the document matters as much as the type.

lines.text: Letter sixty days, bills ninety days.
Originals only for identity.
Two residency documents.

narration.text: To wrap up the documents, here is what to remember. Social Security numbers are collected to verify legal presence and help with child support, and without a number you bring an ineligibility letter no more than sixty days old. Legal presence can be shown with a certified birth certificate, a valid passport or the listed certificates and cards. Names and birth dates should match, and name changes need legal proof. Identity proof must be original, with an out-of-state license usable if expired less than four years. Residency needs two documents, with bills from the last ninety days.
